title: The last four quarters in narrative form
body:
## The Year That Wrote Down a Century

Unitika's fiscal year ending March 2025 produced two numbers that seem, at first glance, to contradict each other. Revenue rose 6.8% to ¥126.4 billion, and operating profit swung from a ¥2.5 billion loss to a ¥5.9 billion gain. Yet the company booked a net loss of ¥24.3 billion — its worst in years — on the back of ¥37.9 billion in impairment charges. The charges were not an accident. Management was deliberately clearing the balance sheet, writing down the fiber and textile assets it had spent a decade failing to fix. The capital adequacy ratio, at 10.4%, left almost no margin for error. Cash and deposits stood at ¥13.5 billion.

The signal inside those numbers was real: the operating businesses were, at last, generating positive cash. The noise — the impairment — was the price of acknowledging what had been obvious for years.

## REVIC and the Transfer of Ownership

Eleven days before the full-year results hit on [May 14, 2025](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news250514.html), Unitika had already crossed the point of no return. On April 30, it cancelled all Class A and Class B preferred shares and issued a new Class C tranche to the state-backed Revival Investment Corporation of Japan (REVIC) via a ¥20 billion third-party allotment. REVIC now controlled 66.76% of voting rights. Separately, Unitika's main lenders — MUFG, Mizuho, and Sumitomo Mitsui Trust — agreed to forgive up to ¥43 billion of debt. The company had not merely restructured its operations; it had restructured its sovereign relationship with capital.

On the May 27 earnings call, incoming CEO Fujii Minoru inherited a company mid-surgery. His messaging centered on three levers: price revisions already embedded in contracts, ongoing cost reduction, and a formal withdrawal from Southeast Asian manufacturing. What he did not offer was a return to the conglomerate model. The fiber and textile businesses, which had consumed management attention for two decades, were explicitly placed in run-off. The session was less a sales pitch than a clinical debrief.

## August: The First Quarter Under New Architecture

The August 6 [Q1 release](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news250806.html) was the first clean read on whether the new structure worked. It was also the self-imposed deadline: management had stated August 2025 as the target for finalizing all divestiture and production-transfer agreements in the structural-reform segments. The data available from the 9-month cumulative suggests the operating machinery was already clicking — Polymers, the highest-margin segment, would eventually deliver ¥7.5 billion in operating profit across nine months on revenue of ¥42.5 billion, a 67% year-on-year improvement. Performance Materials was the second-quarter story, but its trajectory was already forming. Whether management met the August divestiture target on time is not confirmed in the available disclosures, but the October announcement of a nonwovens buyer suggests the pipeline was clearing.

## November: The Company Split

The [H1 results on November 11](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news251111.html) arrived one week after a more consequential document. On November 4, Unitika filed a [notice of company split agreement](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news251104.html) with a wholly-owned subsidiary — the legal mechanism for ring-fencing and transferring a business unit. The split formalized what the restructuring plan had promised: Unitika was not simply selling assets piecemeal but creating distinct legal entities to enable clean ownership transfers. Three consolidated subsidiaries — Unitika Garment Technology, Unitika Spinning, and PT. Unitika Trading Indonesia — were already excluded from the FY3/26 scope by the time the nine-month figures were compiled.

## February: Dissecting the Extraordinary Mix

The February 5–6 [Q3 release](https://www.unitika.co.jp/e/news/news260206.html) is the most complex document in the sequence and requires the closest reading. Nine-month cumulative revenue was ¥95.6 billion, up only 2.2% — a figure that understates the operational shift because the comparison base still includes divested businesses. Operating profit, at ¥9.0 billion, had more than doubled year-on-year (+110.3%). Net income came in at ¥10.6 billion, against a prior-year loss of ¥24.4 billion.

The composition of that net income number should give investors pause. The extraordinary items disclosed were: a ¥23.7 billion gain on sale of non-current assets, partially offset by ¥12.4 billion in business restructuring expenses, with an additional ¥940 million FX valuation gain. Net extraordinary income: ¥11.3 billion. Strip that out, and the underlying result is respectable but far less dramatic.

| Period | Revenue (¥B) | Operating Profit (¥B) | Net Income (¥B) | Equity Ratio |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|-----------------|--------------|
| FY3/24 | 118.3 | -2.5 | -5.4 | n/a |
| FY3/25 | 126.4 | +5.9 | -24.3 | 10.4% |
| 9M FY3/26 | 95.6 | +9.0 | +10.6 | 25.2% |
| FY3/26 guidance | 110.0 | +9.5 | +20.0 | — |

Management also revised full-year guidance in February: revenue cut to ¥110 billion, a 13% decline, while net income guidance was raised to ¥20 billion. Revenue falling and earnings rising is the arithmetic of a divestiture program working as intended. The equity ratio's recovery — from 10.4% at March 2025 to 25.2% nine months later — reflects the REVIC injection and the cash from asset sales. Cash and deposits jumped ¥44.5 billion to reach ¥57.9 billion. The balance sheet, once precarious, now looks rebuilt.

## The April Signal

The April 6 press release ([re20260406-02](https://www.unitika.co.jp/news/io-pdf/re20260406-02.pdf)) falls within the frozen window but its contents remain unverified from available sources. Given the timing — roughly year-end plus ten days — it likely addresses either the Q4 or full-year FY3/26 preliminary figures, or further divestiture mechanics. What the cadence of the prior three quarters establishes is a management team that has been consistent in execution relative to its restructuring promises, even if the headline earnings narrative is substantially a function of asset sales rather than organic operating improvement. That distinction will matter considerably more in FY3/27, when the one-time gains will be exhausted and the trimmed portfolio will have to stand on its own.
